blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define a recession, trace its causes and consequences, and show what a recession does to an economy's position on its production possibility curve.

blocks.heading: What a recession is
blocks.text: A recession is a period in which real GDP falls for two successive quarters or longer, so total output is contracting rather than growing. A fall in one quarter alone does not yet meet the definition; the test is duration as well as direction.

blocks.heading: How a recession begins
blocks.text: A recession often begins on the demand side: households cut spending as incomes or confidence fall, firms delay investment as sales weaken, and export orders drop as customers abroad buy less, as export-led economies such as Germany's find when foreign orders fall away. The fall then feeds itself: total demand falls, so firms cut production and lay off workers, so incomes fall further and demand falls again. A second route runs through finance: where a banking crisis makes loans scarce and costly, firms that depend on credit cut back fast.

blocks.heading: Inside the production possibility curve
blocks.text: On a production possibility curve, a recession is a movement inward, not a shift. In words: two goods on the axes, the curve showing what the economy produces at full use of resources, and the economy first at a point on the curve. As output falls, the economy slides to a point inside the curve: the boundary has not moved, but the economy now produces below what it could, and the gap between curve and point is output the recession wastes - idle workers and machines.

blocks.heading: A consequence is not a cause
blocks.text: Asked why a recession happened, learners often offer what it caused - rising unemployment, firms' losses - as though these brought it about. Causes come before the downturn and produce it; consequences follow from it. To tell them apart, ask whether the item itself needs the recession to have happened first.

blocks.heading: Who a recession hits
blocks.text: The consequences land unevenly: workers lose jobs and incomes; firms lose sales and some fail; the government's tax revenue falls as benefit spending rises, squeezing its budget from both ends; consumers meet a narrower choice as businesses cut back.

blocks.heading: Connections
